title: typedef and readable type names
learningObjectives: Explain the concept and its C rules.
Trace the example and identify data or resource flow.
Recognize relevant safety and failure cases.
Apply the concept in a tested C program.

understand.concept: typedef introduces an alias for an existing type; it does not create a distinct new type. It can make complex declarations, structure names and function pointer types easier to read.
understand.whyItMatters: Readable aliases can simplify interfaces, but excessive or misleading aliases may hide important type information.
understand.analogy: Treat each object or stream as a resource with a defined lifetime and explicit rules for access.
understand.analogyLimit: The analogy does not replace C's formal object, storage-duration, alignment or library rules.

explain.narrative:
typedef introduces an alias for an existing type; it does not create a distinct new type. It can make complex declarations, structure names and function pointer types easier to read.

Check all allocation, I/O and conversion results. Respect object bounds and lifetime, initialize data before reading it, and define who owns and releases each resource.

examples.title: Focused C example
examples.explanation: ItemCount is an alias for unsigned long. Point is an alias for the anonymous structure type. The aliases improve readability but do not create new incompatible types.

practise.guidedTask: Identify which names are aliases and what types they represent.
practise.independentTask: Define aliases for a structure and a callback pointer. Explain how the aliases affect readability and type checking.
hints: typedef does not make two otherwise compatible types distinct.
Use aliases to clarify domain meaning or reduce genuinely complex declarations.
Keep the underlying type visible in documentation when width or signedness matters.
